True, the present Prime Minister in a meeting at Toronto, if I mistake not, did give expression to sentiments 10 p.m. somewhat similar to those contained in that speech and say something about a chart and a compass. Well, I have sometimes thought that the compass which guided his party was very peculiarly constructed. I have always regarded a compass as an instrument whose needle points steadily towards the magnetic north, but I venture to say, after considering what has occurred this session, and after giving consideration to the utterances of the Minister of Finance regarding his attitude on reciprocity, and after hearing what fell this afternoon from the lips of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who very frankly announced that reciprocity with the United States was the goal to be aimed at by his party, and that it must sooner or later come into effect-and he intimated that in his opinion it would be rather sooner than later,-I think in view of all these things we would be justified in noting the fact that this compass which guides and directs the course of hon. gentlemen opposite, rather than indicating the true north, has veered round under the influence of some constellation which rises above the Capitol at Washington. I think, Mr. Speaker, that once it sinks into the consciousness of the people of this country that the policy which they denounced so emphatically in 1911, when by an avalanche of votes they swept the reciprocity proposals into what a good many of us thought would be oblivion, when it is known that those proposals are to be brought to the fore and become the prime policy and guiding star of our friends across the way, I believe that the same verdict will, be given even in a still more unmistakable manner than in 1911. For, surely, if it was justifiable then for the people to turn down those proposals, how much more justifiable is it to-day? In those days our financial situation was greatly different from what it is to-day. We did not need to raise from the tariff, for revenue purposes, anything like the sum it is requisite for us to raise in order to meet our requirements to-day. Then we did not have a great railway problem on our hands, and it was not our duty so essentially as it is today to foster and develop by every possible means traffic east and west along that line of communication rather than north and south. More than that, we did not have such a tremendous trade balance against us as we have now, and we were not in so good a position to judge of the effects which an increased adverse trade balance, by importing largely from the United States, would have upon our financial position. So I say, whatever may have been the verdict in 1911, if a man keeps his ear to the ground to-day, as I suppose so astute a politician as the Minister of Finance does, I should greatly wonder if he has not heard already indistinct rumblings that would indicate that any policy such as he cherishes so dearly would not find acceptance with the people of this country.
I was going to say that my principal objection to his budget proposals rested in the elimination from the Customs Act of the amendment passed last year giving us a dumping clause, as it was known, which was really effective. I have in my hand a telegram received only a few moments ago from the Traffic and Credit Men's Association of British Columbia, one of the largest handlers of produce and fruit in British Columbia. It reads as follows:
Press reports state Fielding proposes eliminate cost production amendment to anti-dumping clause on ground that it constitutes an unne-

The Budget-Mr. MacKelvie
cessary interference with trade. Please wire reply exact position more especially as to whether he raised any objection on principle; also advise full what possible action we can take; also if any alternative protection suggested ; also what is attitude progressives. Very keen interest in matter here. Much depends on your reply.
Naturally enough, knowing the attitude assumed by the Minister of Finance last session when this Parliament enacted that amendment, I gave expression to my view luring the campaign last autumn that if the Liberal party came to power they would not keep that measure of protection on the statute book. I was ridiculed by my opponent, a Liberal gentleman, who thought he had the confidence of the party in that respect, and he said that it was wildly absurd to think that any interference with the customs tariff or the dumping clause would be for one moment contemplated by the party which he represented, if they attained power. The election came on, and that gentleman was not successful in obtaining a seat, but his apprehensions and the apprehensions of his party, and of every board of trade, every commercial organization, every fruit shipping concern, practically every city council in the whole length and breadth of the Okanagan and adjoining valleys, were raised to a pitch of excitement over the dumping clause. The result was that a deputation was sent to Ottawa by the associated boards of trade of that valley, headed by my opponent and another gentleman, Mr. Cossitt, of Vernon, president of the Yale Liberal Association. That deputation interviewed the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau), and possibly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). They stayed here a few days, and on reaching home announced to the press that, after interviewing the Government at Ottawa, they had the assurance that the dumping clause would not be interfered with. Do you wonder at the British Columbia Traffic Association asking me in despair, "What will we do about it"? I will be compelled to say "I do not know." I can make the protest and will present to the Minister of Finance a plea in as strong language as I am capable of presenting, that if he wishes to do anything to injure an industry in which about forty million dollars are involved in the way of investment, and in which a great number of men, women and children are employed, an industry which exported goods to the value of $8,000,000 from that valley to other parts of Canada and abroad this year, 
and if he wishes to handicap their operation and make it more difficult-and goodness knows it is difficult enough to pursue these operations in the Okanagan and other sections of that province-then let him maintain his resolution to do away with the dumping clause. If, on the other hand, he has any desire, as I believe he has, to build up that industry and to give the people there some prospect of success in their endeavours, I plead with him not to maintain his resolution. I am not asking this as a matter of politics, for politically it would be a personal advantage to me to have this provision maintained as it has been announced in the budget, but I would a hundredfold rather throw away any political advantage that would come to me than to see the future of this great industry jeopardized, as it will undoubtedly be, by the proposal contained in the Finance Minister's budget.
I may say to my friends to my left that the success of this business has been very largely built up along lines of co-operation, which, I believe, they consider the proper means of conducting public affairs, as far as possible. The large bulk of the fruit is shipped by co-operative associations grouped together and selling their stuff through the agency of one central consignment association called the Okanagan United Growers, and no greater blow can be inflicted upon the spirit of co-operation than to maintain the proposal of the Finance Minister to abolish that clause in the Customs Act. A dumping clause in the Customs Act, I think, was introduced by the present Minister of Finance away back about 1903 or 1904, and for years we tried to make it effective, but without avail. There were a dozen ways of camouflaging the situation. Goods were sent in on consignment, goods were invoiced improperly, and in a score of ways we found that our efforts were rendered futile, and that we might as well give up any hope of relief from the old dumping clause. Pressure was brought to bear upon the previous government to give us a dumping clause that would really act, and, as a result, in the Customs Act of last year a clause was inserted, the provisions of which, briefly, were that, instead of basing the consideration of the cost of an article upon the marketing price in the place of production, it should be based upon the cost of production where it originated and the customs officer in any locality in Canada was given this privilege; if goods were sent in

The Budget-Mr. MacKelvie
to be sold at a ridiculously low price in competition with home grown products, the customs officer could immediately ascertain what the cost of that product was at point of shipment, add the freight to that charge to bring it to the point where it was offered for sale, and then he was authorized to put on an extra customs impost, to bring it up to a reasonable selling price
The Finance Minister seems to labour under the misapprehension that it was a very difficult act to enforce, and that the poor customs officer was subjected to all kinds of hardships in ascertaining the selling price. I do not know how it would operate in all commodities, but, as far as it affects the fruit industry, it was a matter of the most absolute simplicity to arrive at the cost of production at the point of origination. We invoked that act at least twice last year, one time when the prairie markets were flooded with pears at a dollar a box. We knew the cost of production in Washington, where the pears originated, within a fraction of a cent. There was no difficulty in ascertaining that. The Credit Association of Washington had figures published week by week which were available to us. I believe they cost $1.96 to produce, without taking into consideration the freight charges. We immediately invoked the dumping clause in the Customs Act, and they were compelled to put these goods on the market at a reasonable price. Of course, a good many of our prairie farmers who think they would receive cheaper food in the way of fruit, if this clause were eliminated, are viewing the matter from a mistaken point of view To the south of British Columbia lie two great fruit producing states, Washington and Oregon They always have a surplus. Their production has exceeded the markets of the country. Their object is to sell their prime extra choice fruit at good prices, and they succeed. In order to do that, they have to get rid of their fancy or choice varieties, grades 2 and 3. They ship those to our prairie markets, and those second and third grade varieties set the price for our No. 1 on the prairie market, because they are acceptable to the average buyer, and we have to put down our No. 1 fruit in competition with their grades 2 and 3. We do not object to that very much, but object to having the market slaughtered by apples being sent there, as they were in 1912, 1913 and 1914, and offered at 40 cents a box, when it cost more than two and a half times that amount to produce them.
We did not get any of those on the prairie.

I have seen apples offered at Calgary at 40 cents a box. Once our fruit growers are driven to desperation and throw up the sponge, as they will have to do if too many hardships are inflicted upon them, they may be ruined. If they tear up their orchards and try to go into some other branch of agriculture, it will take years because they cannot Change their business without a sacrifice of a great deal of capital and a considerable amount of time. Once that happens and the markets of the prairies are controlled by the American fruit grower, I venture to say there will be no more cheap fruit. We do not ask a protection that has the effect of raising the cost of food on the prairies. The history of the business shows that protection has not had that effect. I will give the House a very convincing example. The cost of Washington and Oregon apples in Regina, or in Winnipeg, Saskatoon or Brandon, or any of the prairie cities last year or this year has been just the same to a cent as to points directly across the line in the two Dakotas. I go further than that and say this: Although the duty on apples was the only duty affected by the change in 1916, when that duty was raised from 11 1-3 cents a box to 30 cents a box, the price of apples did not advance in anything like the same proportion as the price of plums, cherries, pears and other fruits, which were not subjected to an increase in protective duty. In spite of the increase in protective duty, the difficulties of the business have increased in a greater ratio. There is a continual fight against insect pests. Farmers have to spray their orchards at all seasons of the year; they have to fertilize, they have to prune and gather the brush, and they have to irrigate at an expenditure of $10, $12, $15 or even $17 an acre. Any person from the prairies who thinks the British Columbia farmer is making an undue profit from the product of his toil, is certainly much mistaken. I, therefore, feel justified in once more placing the case before the attention of the Government and asking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) if he cannot make inquiries in an endeavour to reach a solution which will give to those people the protection which I believe they are amply justified in asking.
I do not care to enlarge very much tonight on the general aspect of the tariff. I cannot fail to note, en passant, though, that the party which was pledged to re-

The Budget

Mr. MacKelvie
trencbment, the party which talks of the tremendous extravagance of the past administration and that told the masses of the tremendous burden of taxation which was placed upon them, have again failed very signally in showing any real disposition, in fact, any remote disposition, to bring down taxation by the very apparent and available means of reducing expenditure. What i's the situation? In some fifty enumerated articles we get a reduction of 21 per cent, and in one or two articles a reduction of 5 per cent in the duty, a reduction that will possibly amount to about $1,000,000 for the current year. On the other hand, we have a sales tax which last year brought in $60,000,000, and it is proposed to increase that sales tax by 50 per cent. What relief is afforded to those masses of the people who were subjected to such horrible taxation, if we are to believe the statements of the present Government while they were in opposition? The masses get $1,000,000 taken off the customs tariff; they get $30,000,000 added on to the sales tax. In other words, the masses have to pay $29,000,000 more this year than they were called upon to pay under the preceding government. Has there been any indication, I ask my hon. friends who sit to my left, of any desire, on the part of any party in this House except the group which sits around me, to effect any reduction, by a policyof retrenchment, in the burden of taxation which rests so heavily upon the people of this country? I leave that question with them. If it has been evident to them, it has not been evident to me.
What about the militia estimates?

I am glad the hon. gentleman mentioned the militia estimates. This great country of Canada with a budget this year of about $466,000,000, has effected, in the Department of Militia and in the Department of Naval Service, a little bit of-what shall I call it?-I cannot call it retrenchment. There has been cut off, anyhow, a million or two, with what results and effects? The present Government have absolutely ruined both services, and I have, in justification for that statement, the expressed pronouncement of the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) when he first brought down his estimate to this House. He told us then, on the advice of responsible officers of his department-and he mentioned the name of one of them, a man held in high esteem

throughout Canada-that the irreducible minimum had been reached in the estimates presented to the House

if those are not his exact words, that is the effect of them-and that under no circumstances could the militia be kept up in anything approaching an efficient manner if any further reduction were made. Then we had the pitiable exhibition of the same hon. gentleman coming to this House a few evenings later, and with a bludgeon held over his head, being compelled to swallow his words. My hon. friend to my left says: "What about the militia?" It happened to be my privilege to-day, while I was passing up Elgin street, to see the cadets of Ottawa training, and the sight was an inspiring one. Yet what heart will be in those cadets from now on, what prospects of continuing that splendid organization will they have, when they know the attitude taken by the Minister of Militia and the present Government towards the magnificent services they are giving to the state and themselves? A man has to approach this matter from the grounds of both personal observation and experience, and from both grounds, I can say that we should not interfere with this cadet organization. When I was a boy, I did not have the advantages which boys have to-day in that respect; but I have always considered myself fortunate to have been able to enter what was called the Grammar School Cadets of St. John, N.B. We had to provide our own uniforms, to do the whole thing ourselves. We were fortunate enough to have the instruction of a retired sergeant-major of the Imperial army who had served through the Indian Mutiny. He was rather a martinet; but he succeeded in instilling into us principles of precision and decision, and he gave us a healthy respect for discipline. This worked inestimable advantages upon the physique of all the boys who attended that school. A few years afterwards I found myself in Calgary, when the NorthWest Rebellion of 1885 broke out. There was a time when the sparsely-settled population of the praires was in danger of being annihilated by the Indians and by those who rose under the banner of Riel, and naturally enough everybody flocked to the standard raised then to bring together a group of men to defend their homes. The little experience which I had acquired as a boy in St. John stood me in wonderfully good stead there, and I have always since then, as I said before, considered that it was very fortunate for

The Budget-Mr. MacKelvie
me that I was subjected to that training in my boyhood days. Yet this is one of the things which the Minister of Militia- I do not believe in his heart he feels like doing this-is compelled to brush aside as a matter of small importance to the people of this country, and as my hon. friend to my left says: "We have a reduction in the militia estimates."
I pointed out in this House the other day what an intolerable injustice was effected upon the Naval Department by the contemplated action of the minister. We have a military college at Esquimalt, and I know a number of boys in my constituency who have received training there with a view to entering the navy as a career. They have been there one, two, three years, and now that opportunity is taken away from them. They must give up their career, although their parents have been put to a heavy expense in launching them upon it. Yet I could not elicit from the minister the slightest degree of consciousness that he or his Government was under any responsibilty for this action. Nevertheless, when I speak of retrenchment all that is suggested to the mind of my hon. friend to my left is that we have cut down the militia estimates, and at a time such as this. I suppose some of us read today the speech delivered in the British House of Commons by that great Imperial statesman, Mr. Lloyd George. I suppose we appreciate the difficulty that confronted him at Genoa, and that most of us were glad-I was intensely glad myself-that once more he came out triumphant with his enemies at home and that, because of the underlying truth and sincerity of every word that he uttered, he was able to swing the House of Commons to a position to which he had so often brought them before. Once more triumph perched upon his banner. If there is one man in this world who has had the responsibilities of conducting the great war particularly heavily on his shoulders in the last few years, it is surely the Prime Minister of Great Britain. And yet to-day he is assuming an attitude which I believe carries with it, perhaps, on the part of the civilized world, more appreciation than even his magnificent efforts as war prime minister evoked. He can now be truly termed an apostle of peace. And it is significant, Mr. Speaker, that in this country of ours, guarded and protected during these years of strife by the British navy, which alone kept us from being overwhelmed by the German invader-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Except the Japanese.

Well, the Japanese
did something on the Pacific coast, but no one will contend that they kept the North Sea free. I was about to say, that it ill becomes us, who have received such protection at the hands of the British navy, to say that, notwithstanding the fact that we are spending more than $50,000,000 more than the Government did last year, we cannot afford a paltry million or two for the army and navy. And this is the Government that was going to retrench. I suppose that on the Pacific coast we have reason to congratulate ourselves, though the situation is no longer as it was. The Anglo-Japanese alliance has been broadened into a four-power alliance, and we can call if necessary upon France and the United States to protect our coast if aggression were now to offer. But this is unnecessary. We can all sleep in security, resting our heads on our pillows at night in the proud consciousness that sweeping up and down the coasts, protecting us from any invader, are the two trawlers so kindly provided by the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham).
Now, not content with tampering with the clause in the Customs Act which gives protection to the fruit industry, we now have the spectacle of a finance minister coming before the House and declaring that the time has again arrived when the inestimable privilege may be enjoyed by the Canadian people of trading freely with the Germans. It is obvious that with the depreciation of the German mark, nominally in times before the war worth 23 cents, and now worth about one-third of a Canadian cent, if you allow goods to come in under valuations of that kind, no customs tariff would afford protection. But we did overcome that difficulty last year when we inserted a clause that gave us that protection by stabilizing the currency at 50 per cent of its value. Now our factories have to be subjected to this competition. Men seeking employment here will have to compete with the German labourer, who, as we were told this afternoon, is willing to work for $3 a month, of our money. I wonder if there are no sentimental reasons that can appeal to this House in this connection. I do not think I am a man who cherishes implacable hatreds; I do not believe that in my constitution there is in any great degree a spirit of vindictiveness; but I can well remember-indeed, Sir, I do not think I am ever likely to

The Budget-Mr. MacKelvie
forget it-that during the war period men and women from one coast to the other in this country denounced German atrocities and brutalities and vowed that never again would they trade with a brutal nation of that kind. I wonder if we are not justified in departing just a little from the cold commercial aspect of the question and giving some slight consideration to the senti * nental view of this matter. There are men and women in this country, of whom I am free to confess that I am one, who are nov inclined to forget that the blood of countless innocent babes and women, and murdered hospital nurses and wounded soldiers who were killed in hospitals, if it does not c-ry for vengeance at our hands, has at least a justifiable claim to remembrance. And i would rather be in the position of a government that tried to exclude a reasonable amount of German goods from coming to this country, than be one to throw down every possible barrier and allow our country to be flooded by the products of people who were our enemies a few years ago and whose ideals are yet very far, I think, from approximating our own.
Well, we come now to the amendment that has been offered. I have said that I oppose this budget primarily because of the injustice it inflicts on the fruit growing industry, in removing a dumping clause which was really effective; and yet I can also sincerely stand behind the resolution moved by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) this afternoon, not, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) indicated, in an effort to obscure the issue, because the party opposite are pursuing a course which I consider objectionable or wrong. It is too late to-day for me to inform the House that I am a protectionist. Protection is one of the fundamentals of my political creed, and I am proud to say that I belong to a party whose political compass has never deviated from the pole in that direction during the whole period of its history. For over half a century we have had a Liberal-Conservative party in Canada, sometimes in power and sometimes out of power. But whether occupying the treasury benches or sitting to the left of the Speaker, they have ever and always maintained, on this important question, an attitude which never left them open to the reproach that they had deserted their flag for one moment. It is not because I am anxious that the party opposite should do what we say they have not done, it is just exactly because of what the resolution

expresses, that I believe they should be censured. Surely the time has arrived, as I said before, when thinking people demand from a great party some policy or pronouncement behind which there is sincerity. But take this document of theirs, this famous declaration of the National (invention, and you see that the ruthless fingers of expediency have gripped it and torn its pages off one by one, scattering them to the four winds of heaven until they litter the ground along with other historical scraps of paper which we have heard so much about during the last few years. In view of this, I feel amply justified in giving my support to the amendment proposed this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I do not feel like making a long speech, but 1 do want	to express my views
upon certain aspects of the budget that has been presented to the House. I have had a bitter disappointment in the budget. We in Alberta have not been asking for free trade at once; we have known that it was not advisable, that perhaps it was not even possible for us to at once enter on a free trade policy. However, we have had fn the backs of our heads, and we have yet, the idea that we want to get a whole lot taken off the tariff and the burdens of our people thus lightened just as soon as possible. Our disappointment is in the slightness of the reduction. It is so small that it would make very little difference in the expense of our living or in the expense of operating our farms. Indeed, in my judgment, it is really not any reduction at all, for if I figure it correctly, our expense will be more instead of less when the sales tax is taken into account. We hoped for a greater reduction. The Liberal sentiment in Alberta has been very strong for years, the Progressive sentiment has been stronger, towards tariff reduction, and about the first thing I would have said to me by a Liberal if I undertook to talk politics to him in the last few years would be, "We have got to have the tariff reduced."
As I have said, we have not been looking for very much-and certainly we have not got very much of a reduction. Last fall, if I might approach the subject, the Liberals tried very hard to get even one seat in Alberta for a cabinet minister. This was an earnest, honest effort on the part of some of the Liberals in that province. But I believe they will have to try a good deal

The Budget-Mr. Warner
harder next time unless they show greater tariff reductions in their next budget. These are prophecies only. I do not like to talk politics, but it looks to me as if the Liberals by this budget had not gone very far towards strengthening themselves in the West.
I have found two articles on which there is a 5 per cent reduction of duty, and only two; all the rest less, mostly two and a half per cent. I find that the British preference on collars and cuffs is increased 5 per cent. Now, the Alberta farmer wants to dress just as well as he can afford to, but one man told me in the last campaign that he had not worn a stiff collar and cuffs for six years. Now then, this 5 per cent off his collars and cuffs is not going to do him much good. I myself have worn them a little oftener than that, but I do not know whether I and others are going to be able to continue to do so unless we have a little better tariff treatment.
There is also, I find, a 5 per cent reduction in the duty on dairy utensils. I had quite a time here a few days ago telling you people how hard it was to carry on the dairy business. I was out against oleomargarine; I am yet, and I would like to see the dairy business get a fair Chance to make good. Our Minister of Finance made a strong appeal for oleomargarine. I suppose he has a tender spot in his heart, and is trying to give us something back as consolation for the hard knocks that he tried to give the dairy business in that speech. Now he is giving our dairy men a 5 per cent reduction in the duty on their dairy equipment, but I think it will be a good, long time before he can convince our dairy men that that is the proper way or sufficient to enable them to compete With oleomargarine.
The Minister of Finance also made a number of remarks regarding the lack of the need of protection of the people regarding the consumption of oleomargarine. We have been protecting the people of this country a long time. As far as I am concerned-I am speaking for myself individually-I know that we have been protecting certain people long enough, and that the farmer and the dairy man deserve a little more protection and a little more consideration than they are getting out of this budget. We have protected the people against certain things, and we have made it compulsory that their children shall go to school. But there is not very much duty taken off the wearing apparel that those
children have to wear in the cold country that we live in. Wool and hides are almost given away in the West at the present time. It is very hard to sell them, and in any case you cannot sell them at a price that is anywhere near the cost of production, and we do not hope to under present conditions. But the duties on woollen goods and shoes are not reduced at all', and the only concession, if I understand aright, is a 2i per cent increase in the British preference. We have a right, I think, to expect a reduction of the duty on woollen and leather goods and other clothing so necessary in our cold climate.
Now, as I said before, I believe that the country must provide the money to run the government. At the same time I do not hear any proposal to increase the income tax. We have seen great fortunes built up during the war, and these we are hardly touching with our income tax. When anyone has an income of from $50,000 to $100,000 a year, it seems to me that we can hit him up a little harder and let off the man who is paying all he can stand and more too for his living and is operating his farm at a loss. I think it would be no hardship to get more revenue from the income tax. It may be said that the farmers are not paying the income tax. Well, I want to tell the House that we would be mighty glad to be in a position to pay the income tax once more. I believe it would be more just and more reasonable to reduce the cost of living to the poor people of this country and to take more by way of income tax and some other lines of taxation which would have somewhat the same effect-that of placing the taxation where the people are able to bear it. It has been said to me that we must allow capital sufficient encouragement to induce it to go into business. I grant that; but if the capital gets all the encouragement and the man who needs the manufactured goods cannot buy them, what will happen then? What is happening now? That is just what is the matter with our country at the present time; the people who should buy these goods have lost their purchasing power and what we must do is enable these people to get their purchasing power back again. We are not asking for anything that we think it is unfair for us to have, but we certainly have been paying these tariff duties long enough, and we feel that there could have been more reduction, not only for our benefit, but for the benefit of the whole of Canada. When

The Budget-Mr. Warner
I came here-and I feel the same yet-I wanted to do everything that was possible to secure good government. I want to encourage the Government in every way that I can, but I want to see this Government consider the people who are unable to buy rather than the people who, perhaps, are not in need of employing their money. We want to see that money employed, but as in the case of our railroads, we want our people to get a chance to .get back on their feet. You cannot do business with people who are not able to buy, and the Government must give consideration to the needs of those people who are the purchasers of all the manufactured goods in the production of which capital is employed.
As far as the British preference is concerned, on the agricultural implements it amounts to little or nothing. Most of the agricultural implements that we buy are made in the United States or at home. Practically all our machinery is made on this side of the water and the British preference does not apply to them. The budget proposes a slight reduction in the duties on farm machinery, but when you put that into a wagon that costs over $100 or a reaper that costs from $280 to $300, you get very little benefit from it. I think the Government might well have gone further in that line and have made up the difference by getting an additional revenue from some of the sources that I have mentioned-from people who are better able to bear it than those from whom it is now proposed to take the money in the form of sales tax. This sales tax is a thing which I confess I do not altogether understand. I do not know just to what extent the sales tax will neutralize the reduction in the tariff, but in my judgment-and it is the opinion of others with whom I have talked on the subject-it will more than neutralize the tariff reductions and will make things cost more instead of less. If that is the case, there is only one saving clause in that feature of it: the treasury, if this tax is collected, will get it instead of the manufacturer. It goes where we want it to go if we have to pay the tax. The hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Woods) this afternoon pointed out that on automobiles made in this country the manufacturer gets an extra price on account of the tariff-from which is deducted, of course, the small amount of sales tax. On the contrary, when we import an automobile, the duty on it goes to the treasury, and we pay the sales tax in addition. Automobiles are not now considered only a luxury; I believe the people

generally look upon them as a necessity. In the case of a farmer who lives twenty miles from town, the automobile has moved him up within five or six miles of town, when you measure the speed of the automobile against the speed of a team in making that distance. The farmers use as few teams as they can; they use their automobile to go to town except when there is heavy hauling to do. The farmer, therefore, feels that he is almost compelled to have an automobile, and the additional sales tax will certainly make the automobile cost him more. In fact, the increase will more than offset the other reductions of which he will obtain the benefit. However, it is unnecessary for me to dwell on this subject; I desire only to make a sort of general survey of the Finance Minister's proposals. I hope that the Government will see fit to do more than is proposed in the present budget toward reducing the cost of living to the farmers and causing them once more to feel that they are going to get a square deal at the hands of the Government.
